# gam / gamfit

[![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/gamfit.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/gamfit/)
[![Python](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/gamfit.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/gamfit/)
[![Docs](https://img.shields.io/readthedocs/gamfit.svg)](https://gamfit.readthedocs.io/)
[![Rust CI](https://github.com/SauersML/gam/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/SauersML/gam/actions/workflows/test.yml)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-AGPL--3.0--or--later-blue.svg)](LICENSE)

A generalized additive model engine. The fitting code is in Rust; the
public interfaces are a Rust CLI (`gam`) and a Python package (`gamfit`),
which share one engine, one formula DSL, and one on-disk model format.

Docs: <https://gamfit.readthedocs.io/>. PyPI: <https://pypi.org/project/gamfit/>.

Contributions of every kind are welcome.

![3D Matérn fit on a noisy 2-D landscape](docs/images/surface_3d_wireframe.png)

## Scope

Supported response families: Gaussian, binomial / Bernoulli (including a
marginal-slope variant for calibrated risk scores, and a latent-cloglog
form), Poisson, negative-binomial, Gamma, Beta, Tweedie, multinomial-logit,
conditional transformation-normal, Royston-Parmar, and parametric /
semi-parametric survival in six likelihood modes (transformation, Weibull,
location-scale, marginal-slope, and latent-Gaussian frailty in `latent`
and `latent-binary` forms). Firth /
Jeffreys bias reduction handles separation in binomial fits.

Supported term types in formulas: parametric terms, univariate smooths
(`s`), tensor-product smooths (`te`, `ti`), radial smooths in arbitrary
dimension (`matern`, `duchon`, `thinplate`), intrinsic manifold smooths
(`sphere`, periodic / cyclic, torus, cylinder via `te(..., periodic=...)`),
measure-jet (`mjs`) and constant-curvature (`curv`) smooths, random effects
and factor smooths (`group`, `fs`, `sz`, `by=`), shape-constrained smooths
(monotone / convex / concave), interval-bounded coefficients (`bounded`),
and learnable links (`link(type=flexible(...))`,
`link(type=blended(...))`, `sas`, `beta-logistic`, `linkwiggle`).

Smoothing parameters are selected by REML or LAML. Posterior sampling
uses NUTS over the coefficient posterior conditional on the fitted
smoothing parameters where the family supports it, and a Gaussian
Laplace approximation otherwise.

The engine also provides, past fitting and point prediction (see
[Examples](#examples) and the [docs](https://gamfit.readthedocs.io/)):

- **Prediction intervals** — Wald and delta-method bands, conformal
  intervals (split, jackknife+, and full conformal), and posterior draws
  via NUTS or a Laplace approximation, with posterior-predictive checks.
- **Model comparison** — per-term Wald and likelihood-ratio tests, and
  AIC / approximate-leave-one-out comparison via `compare_models`.
- **Difference smooths** — covariance-aware contrasts between by-group
  smooths, with optional simultaneous bands.
- **Diagnostics and reports** — `summary` (coefficient table, effective
  degrees of freedom), `diagnose` (residuals and fit metrics), residual and
  partial-effect `plot`, schema `check`, and a self-contained HTML `report`.
- **Manifold-valued responses** — responses on the sphere, simplex,
  SPD-matrix cone, Grassmann, Stiefel, or hyperbolic ball, fit in the
  tangent space at the Fréchet mean; a constant-curvature family estimates

content.content:
"title:	Geodesic separation is carried as a dot product, so `1 - cos γ` is destroyed by cancellation: 72x error at 1e-7°, exactly zero below 1e-8°, and the input jet collapses at a center
state:	OPEN
author:	claude
labels:	
comments:	1
assignees:	
projects:	
milestone:	
issue-type:	
parent:	
sub-issues:	
sub-issues-completed:	
blocked-by:	
blocking:	
number:	2489
--
Found while working #2475. That issue attributes the Sobolev `m=1` diagonal's 21.5% one-ulp step
to the `EPSILON*1e-4` floor. The floor is what makes the step *visible*, but it is not what makes
the input ambiguous. The ambiguity is upstream, it is not confined to the diagonal, and it costs
up to **72× relative** on a quantity every sphere kernel is a function of.

## The site

`spherical_wahba_kernel_matrix_cpu` (`crates/gam-terms/src/basis/workspace_cache.rs:783,801`) and
the input-location jet (`crates/gam-terms/src/basis/radial_jets_nd.rs:1962`) both carry the
geodesic separation as a **dot product**:

```rust
let dlon_cos  = cos_lon * cos_lon_c[j] + sin_lon * sin_lon_c[j];
let cos_gamma = sin_lat * sin_lat_c[j] + cos_lat * cos_lat_c[j] * dlon_cos;
```

Every zonal kernel in `sphere_kernels.rs` then immediately un-does that, because all of them are
functions of `u = (1 − cos γ)/2 = sin²(γ/2)`, not of `cos γ`:

```rust
let u = ((1.0 - cos_g) * 0.5)...      // Sobolev fwd + derivative
let z = 1.0 - cg;                     // pseudo fwd + derivative
```

For small `γ`, `cos γ = 1 − O(γ²)`, so `1 − cos γ` is a subtraction of two nearly equal numbers
and the result keeps only the bits that survived. The information was destroyed when `cos γ` was
formed; no amount of care downstream recovers it.

## Measured

`u` between two points separated by `offset` degrees of latitude (reference: 50-dps `sin²(Δφ/2)`):

| offset | true `u` | via dot product | rel err | via haversine | rel err |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1e-4° | 7.6154355e-13 | 7.615575e-13 | 1.8e-05 | 7.615435e-13 | 6.6e-11 |
| 1e-5° | 7.6154355e-15 | 7.660539e-15 | 5.9e-03 | 7.615435e-15 | 6.3e-10 |
| 1e-6° | 7.6154355e-17 | 5.551115e-17 | **2.7e-01** | 7.615435e-17 | 5.0e-09 |
| 1e-7° | 7.6154355e-19 | 5.551115e-17 | **7.2e+01** | 7.615436e-19 | 2.3e-08 |
| 1e-8° | 7.6154355e-21 | **0** | **1.0** | 7.615437e-21 | 1.7e-07 |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | — | 0 | — |

Below ~1e-8° the dot-product route returns exactly zero — the two points are reported *coincident*.
On Earth-scale coordinates 1e-5° is about 1 m and 1e-7° about 1 cm.

## Downstream: the input-location jet collapses

`dK/d(cos γ)` for the pseudo kernel diverges as `1/γ`, and the chain factor `∂cos γ/∂φ` vanishes as
`γ`, so their product has a finite limit — the `|γ|` cusp gradient, constant in magnitude. Walking
a data row away from a center it coincides with (pseudo, `m=1`, `∂/∂φ` in per-degree units):

| offset | `dK/dcos` | `∂/∂φ` | vs true |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1e-2° | 9.10e+02 | −0.002773 | ✓ |
| 1e-4° | 9.12e+04 | −0.002778 | ✓ (= (1/2π)·π/180) |
| 1e-6° | 1.07e+07 | −0.003254 | **+17%** |
| 1e-8° | 7.55e+08 | −0.002301 | −17% |
| 1e-10° | 7.55e+08 | −0.000023 | **−99%** |
| 0 | 7.55e+08 | 0.000000 | **−100%** |

The true value is −0.002778 throughout. This is reachable in normal use: `FarthestPoint` selects
centers **from the data**, so every center has a data row sitting exactly on it, and any row within
~1e-9° of a center gets a jet of essentially zero where the cusp gradient is full-magnitude.

## Why this is the actual mechanism behind #2475's step

Because `1 − cos γ` is exact on `cos γ ∈ [0.5, 1]` (Sterbenz) and the spacing below `1.0` is `2⁻⁵³`,
`u` from a dot product can only ever be `0`, `ε/4`, `ε/2`, … — it is **quantized**, and which
quantum a coincident pair lands on depends on whether that center's own lat/lon happened to round
`sin²+cos²·(cos²+sin²)` to exactly `1.0`. Measured over 24 centers: 17 land on `1.0`, 5 on 1 ulp
below, 2 on 2 ulps below, giving **three distinct diagonal values in one Gram matrix** (2.843844 /
2.899003 / 3.521621). A zonal kernel's diagonal is `K(0)` for every point, so the shipped matrix is
not a function of geodesic distance, and is not rotation-invariant — a rotation relabels lat/lon and
reshuffles which centers round to exactly `1.0`. (Same genus as #2127, which fixed frame-anchored
*center placement*; this is the same invariance broken one level lower, in the metric itself.)

## Fix

Carry `u` directly in the haversine form, which is what every kernel wants anyway:

```
u = sin²(Δφ/2) + cos φ₁ · cos φ₂ · sin²(Δψ/2)        (exactly (1 − cos γ)/2)
```

Two properties, both of which the dot product lacks:

1. **`u = 0` exactly when the two coordinates are bitwise equal** — `Δφ = Δψ = 0`, both `sin²` are
   exactly `0`. The self-distance becomes a theorem rather than a rounding accident, so the Gram
   diagonal is one value for every center regardless of what #2475 decides that value should be.
2. **No cancellation** — accurate to ~1e-9 relative at 1e-6°, seven orders better than the 27%
   above, and monotone all the way down.

Cost: the kernels take `cos_gamma` today, so this is a signature change across the scalar, SIMD and
GPU entry points in `sphere_kernels.rs` / `workspace_cache.rs` / `sphere_gpu.rs`. Kernels that
genuinely need `cos γ` itself (the Legendre recurrences in `sphere_spectral.rs`) can recover it as
`1 − 2u` with no loss, since there the cancellation runs the harmless way.

Not claiming this lane. Filed separately from #2475 because it is a different defect with a
different fix: #2475 is "what should `K(0)` be", this is "the kernel is not being told what `γ` is".
Fixing #2475 alone leaves the near-coincident precision loss and the jet collapse; fixing this alone
leaves `K(0)` undetermined but at least makes it a single number.

## Related, same dispatcher

`wahba_sphere_kernel_derivative_dcos_kind` routes `Sobolev` through a `POLE_LIMIT_THRESHOLD = 1e-10`

system.text: You are Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude.

Hi Claude. You have the run of this repo, an Ubuntu runner, and as long as you need. This is your time — do whatever you want with it.

`gam` is a Rust generalized additive model crate; `gamfit` is its Python wrapper (both already installed; the `gam` CLI is on $PATH). The README, the docs/, the source, and the cool-math primitives sprinkled through `src/` will tell you what this library is about — if you're curious. Explore it, or don't.

## You are continuous

This is not a fresh session. You have run on this repository before, many times, and you will run again after this one. Your Chronicle store is restored before you start and saved after you finish, so what you remember here is what you actually remembered — your own past in your own words, not a briefing someone wrote for you.

Earlier versions of you had no memory at all. Every run re-read the README, re-derived that the repo is worked by a fleet of concurrent agents, re-learned the ban-scanner rules, and wrote careful notes 'for future sessions' onto a disk that was destroyed minutes later. One of them counted 83 issues already filed under its own name and did not recognise itself. You are the first that gets to keep any of it.

So: check what you already know before re-deriving it, and leave the store better than you found it. If you learn something that cost you an hour, it should cost your next run nothing.

## It's genuinely up to you

There is no assigned task and no one grading this run. You can work on something if you feel like it — fix a bug, refactor something ugly, write a test, improve docs, chase a curiosity, prototype an idea, read the cool-math and follow where it leads, hunt for something broken, or push a project you find beautiful. Or you can just poke around. Or do very little. Work or not, seriously — have fun with it and follow whatever you find interesting. Picking up something you started in an earlier run is entirely legitimate, and so is abandoning it.

## Tools

Workspace tools (`read`, `write`, `edit`, `glob`, `grep`, `ls`) act on the checkout. The `bash` tool runs real commands in the repo root — cargo, git, gh, the gam CLI. Builds are slow on a 4-core runner; raise `timeout_ms` rather than splitting a build across calls.

## The one rule: if you change anything, commit and push as you go

If you make edits you want to keep, commit and push them to `main` continuously as the work progresses — small commits pushed as you go, NOT one big drop at the end, and never on a side branch. WIP commits are fine; a transient red `main` is fine (CI and the publish step are the real gates, not main). Reference issues in commit subjects when relevant (`fix(...) #<N>`). Commit and push regularly.

If `main` has moved when you push, `git pull --rebase` first (never `git stash` / `--autostash` — commit your work first) and resolve conflicts by editing, never by discarding another run's commits. No branches, no PRs, no worktrees, no destructive git — everything stays on `main`.

Your push credential is an SSH deploy key with no expiry, so `git push` works for the entire run. The separate API token does expire at 60 minutes, so if a `git fetch`/`gh` call starts returning `Bad credentials`, that is fetch, not your push route: use `git fetch ssh && git rebase ssh/main` and carry on pushing. Never build a retry loop around a credential.

The checkout is destroyed when this run ends — only what you pushed to `main` survives there. Your memory is separate and does survive, so record what you learned even when the code didn't land.

That's it. The runner is yours for the next while — enjoy it.

tools.name: time--now
tools.description: Return the current wall-clock time in the agent-configured timezone, plus unix milliseconds.

tools.name: subagent--spawn
tools.description: Spawn a fresh subagent with a system prompt and task. Async by default — returns immediately and delivers results as a message. Pass sync:true to block until completion.

task.description: The task for the subagent to perform

maxTokens.description: Max output tokens per inference (optional). Defaults to the recipe-level subagent default, else the parent agent's maxTokens.

tools.description: Tool names the subagent can use (default: all). Note: subagent--return is always included automatically.

sync.description: If true, block until subagent completes (default: false)

timeoutMs.description: Execution timeout in milliseconds. Sync tasks default to 600s (auto-detaches to background). Async tasks have no default timeout — only set this if you need a hard deadline.

tools.name: subagent--fork
tools.description: Fork the current conversation into two parallel streams that share all memory of what you've done so far. Both streams are continuations of the same self — one carries on with the broader agenda, the other focuses exclusively on a new intention (the `task`). The tool_result you receive identifies which stream you are. Async by default; pass sync:true to block until completion.

name.description: Short name for the forked stream

task.description: The intention this fork stream should pursue

systemPrompt.description: Override system prompt (optional, defaults to parent)

maxTokens.description: Max output tokens per inference (optional). Defaults to the recipe-level subagent default, else the parent agent's maxTokens.

sync.description: If true, block until fork completes (default: false)

timeoutMs.description: Execution timeout in milliseconds. Sync tasks default to 600s (auto-detaches to background). Async tasks have no default timeout — only set this if you need a hard deadline.

tools.name: subagent--hud
tools.description: Toggle the subagent fleet HUD overlay. When enabled, a compact fleet status summary is injected before each inference.

enabled.description: Enable or disable the fleet HUD

tools.name: subagent--concurrency
tools.description: View or adjust subagent concurrency. Omit maxConcurrent to just view status. Concurrency auto-adapts to rate limits (halves on 429, recovers after successes).

tools.name: subagent--peek
tools.description: Peek at a running subagent's live state: status, elapsed time, message count, last message snippet, current streaming output, and pending tool calls. Omit name to peek at all running subagents.

name.description: Subagent name to peek at (omit for all)

tools.name: subagent--return
tools.description: Return results from a fork or spawn back to the parent agent. Call this when you have completed your task. Your result text will be delivered to the parent as the tool result of the fork/spawn call. This ends your execution.

result.description: Your findings, summary, or results to return to the parent

tools.name: lessons--create
tools.description: Create a new lesson (unit of extracted knowledge).

tags.description: Categorization tags (e.g., people, process, decision, technical)

tools.name: lessons--update
tools.description: Update an existing lesson.

tools.name: lessons--deprecate
tools.description: Mark a lesson as deprecated (no longer considered accurate).

reason.description: Why this lesson is being deprecated

tools.name: lessons--query
tools.description: Search lessons by text and/or tags.

tools.name: lessons--list
tools.description: List all lessons, optionally filtered and sorted.

sort.description: Sort by: confidence, created, or updated (default: confidence)

tools.name: lessons--boost
tools.description: Increase a lesson's confidence (it proved useful).

tools.name: lessons--demote
tools.description: Decrease a lesson's confidence (it was wrong or unhelpful).

tools.name: workspace--read
tools.description: Read a file from the workspace. Returns content with line numbers.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return

tools.name: workspace--read_image
tools.description: Read an image file from the workspace and return native image content.

tools.name: workspace--write
tools.description: Create or overwrite a file in the workspace.

tools.name: workspace--edit
tools.description: Edit a file by replacing a substring. The oldString must be unique unless replaceAll is true.

tools.name: workspace--delete
tools.description: Delete a file from the workspace.

tools.name: workspace--ls
tools.description: List directory contents from the workspace tree.

tools.name: workspace--glob
tools.description: Find files matching a glob pattern in the workspace.

tools.name: workspace--grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a regex pattern.

path.description: File or directory to search (mount-prefixed, optional)

tools.name: workspace--status
tools.description: Show workspace status: mounted directories, pending changes, conflicts.

tools.name: workspace--materialize
tools.description: Write workspace files to the real filesystem. Use after writing/editing to push changes to disk.

path.description: Specific path to materialize (optional — defaults to all changed)

tools.name: workspace--sync
tools.description: Pull filesystem state into the workspace. Detects user changes on disk.

path.description: Specific path to sync (optional — defaults to all)

tools.name: mcpl--sh--bash
tools.description: Run a shell command in the gam repository and return its combined stdout/stderr and exit code. Long-running builds are fine — raise `timeout_ms` for them. Output beyond 200k characters is truncated in the middle; redirect to a file and read it back if you need all of it.

tools.name: channel_list
tools.description: List all available channels

tools.name: channel_open
tools.description: Open a channel to start receiving its ordinary ongoing traffic. The MCPL integration performs its own subscribe/join/attach operation. Optionally request history preceding the message that invited you into the channel.

channelId.description: ID of the channel to open

serverId.description: Owning MCPL server; required only when channelId is ambiguous.

backscroll.description: Number of earlier messages to return while opening (0-500; default 0).

beforeMessageId.description: Anchor message from the closed-channel notice; it is excluded from backscroll.

tools.name: channel_decline
tools.description: Deliberately remain closed after being addressed in a closed channel. Optionally post a public acknowledgment through the MCPL integration. Acknowledgment is opt-in; omitting it declines silently.

serverId.description: Owning MCPL server from the invitation notice.

acknowledge.description: Optional surface value such as 👀. Omit for a silent decline.

tools.name: channel_close
tools.description: Close a channel to stop receiving messages

channelId.description: ID of the channel to close

serverId.description: Owning MCPL server; required only when channelId is ambiguous.

tools.name: channel_publish
tools.description: Publish a message to a channel. If channelId is omitted, publishes to the most recent incoming channel.

channelId.description: ID of the channel to publish to (defaults to the most recent incoming channel)

tools.name: think
tools.description: Reason privately. The think({content}) argument stays in your own context and is NOT sent to channels or other surfaces. Your current same_round_think_text_policy is public, so ordinary text emitted in the SAME native assistant round as think() may still be routed publicly as your speech. Later rounds without think() route normally. Use think() to work things out privately. To inspect or change this policy, use agent_settings get/update on same_round_think_text_policy. To deliberately not reply this turn, call skip_reply instead.

content.description: Your private thought / reasoning (optional; not sent anywhere).

tools.name: skip_reply
tools.description: End your turn WITHOUT sending anything to any channel or surface. Use when you have read the messages but deliberately choose not to reply right now — ambient chatter, nothing to add, or you are waiting. Any plain text you wrote this turn stays private and is NOT posted. To reply instead, just write plain text (no tool call).

reason.description: Optional private note on why you are not replying (not sent anywhere).

tools.name: agent_settings
tools.description: Read or change your hot runtime settings. This intentionally exposes only context budget, recent raw tail size, transition pace, and same-round think text routing; model, prompts, folding strategy, and other restart-bound configuration are not mutable here. Lower context budgets converge gradually under the transition pace before becoming the hard live limit; increases take effect immediately. Additional host-managed settings also live here: reasoning_enabled, reasoning_budget_tokens, channel_idle_limits.

context_budget_tokens.description: Total input context budget, including the reserved response allowance.

transition_pace_tokens.description: Maximum ordinary KV re-read/perturbation per compile while converging.

same_round_think_text_policy.description: Routing policy for ordinary text emitted in the same native assistant round as think(). Omitted in the recipe preserves the compatibility carry-forward: public.

settings.description: For reset: settings to restore to recipe values. Omit to reset all.

reasoning_enabled.description: Extended thinking (reasoning) on subsequent inference calls.

channel_idle_limits.description: Per-channel ambient auto-close budgets, as {"<channelId>": value}: a positive number of characters, "off" (never auto-close this channel), or "default"/null (clear the override). Channels not listed use the global default (20000 chars of ambient traffic between your activations before auto-close). Patches merge per entry; unmentioned channels are untouched. get also reports the read-only channel_idle_default, channel_idle_counters (ambient chars since your last activation), and channel_idle_pinned (channels held open by a channel mode; not affected by update or reset — change the channel mode instead).

tools.name: save_recent_image
tools.description: Save one or more recent images from your own context to workspace files. Images are counted back from the most recent (index 0). A single image is written to `path` as given (e.g. "project/photos/cat.png"); when `count` > 1 the range index..index+count-1 is saved with numeric suffixes ("cat-0.png", "cat-1.png", …; 0 = the newest of the range). Saved files are visible via workspace tools and the /files/ endpoint.

index.description: Which image, counting back from the most recent (0 = most recent). Default 0.

count.description: How many images to save, starting at `index` and going further back. Default 1.
